title: Agent contract (contracts/<agent-name>.yaml)
description: The machine-readable declaration of one agent: what it must be given, what it must produce, what it may never do, and what it is allowed to touch. Before this existed those rules were spread across the agent's own prompt, CLAUDE.md and policies/*.md, where nothing could check them. The orchestrator's in-process registry is checked against these files, so the two can never drift apart silently.

role.description: The `--agent` value passed to the claude CLI, which resolves .claude/agents/<role>.md. Equal to name by design: one identifier, not a mapping to keep in sync.

required.description: Artifacts the agent cannot start without. A missing one is a reason to stop, never a reason to guess.

optional.description: Artifacts the agent reads when they exist — e.g. a previous QA round, or its own prior code.

constraints.description: Hard boundaries, as identifiers rather than prose, so they can be checked instead of only read. Each traces to a rule in policies/*.md.

capabilities.description: The fixed permission vocabulary the orchestrator enforces today.

read.description: Paths this role's run actually needs to read, from CLAUDE.md's Reads column and policies/documentation.md 10. Unlike write/deny this is NOT enforced as a block: reading is non-destructive, and a read guard that got a path wrong would trap an agent mid-run for no safety gain. It is documentation the orchestrator can act on -- it says what to assemble into a prompt, and checkPathRules() holds it to one real rule: everything a role may write, it must also be able to read, because a document you cannot open is a document you cannot amend.

write.description: Path globs this agent may write. Empty carries the same meaning as `read` above.

deny.description: Paths this agent must never write, even when a write glob would otherwise match. Subtractive on purpose: a broad allow plus a narrow deny is far easier to read (and to get right) than an allow list that has to enumerate every exception. Globs support * within a segment and ** across segments.

capability.description: What this agent can actually build, as opposed to where it sits in the pipeline (T12). Role says which stage; this says which work. The two were the same thing only while there was exactly one stack — a backend-engineer that knows Express and Prisma is not interchangeable with one that knows EF Core. Empty arrays are meaningful: an analysis role genuinely writes no language, which is different from not having been filled in.

capabilities.description: A closed vocabulary, because a capability exists to be matched and free text cannot be matched reliably — rest-api, REST API and restful would read as three different things, and a typo would read as "nobody can do this".

states.description: The task states this agent is allowed to act in.
